solutions.text: The passage explicitly states that gut microbes synthesise vitamin K and several B vitamins, that antibiotics transiently reduce diversity, that transplants transfer metabolic traits between mice, and that diet reshapes the community within days. It makes no claim anywhere about treating or curing inflammatory bowel disease with probiotic supplements, so that statement goes beyond the text. The probiotic claim is plausible-sounding health advice, but plausibility is not support: nothing in the passage links probiotics to any disease outcome.

The council infers causation from a correlation. If tree-lined streets are concentrated in wealthier neighbourhoods, then wealth plausibly drives both the tree planting and the lower asthma (better housing, healthcare, lower pollution exposure), so planting more trees need not change asthma rates at all: this confounder attacks the inference directly. By contrast, the fact that trees produce pollen, or that asthma has many triggers, does not explain why tree-rich areas show less asthma, so neither undermines the conclusion as strongly.

Italy has previously hosted the Winter Games at Cortina d'Ampezzo in 1956 and in Turin in 2006. Milano Cortina 2026 is therefore the third Italian Winter Olympics. Calling it the first or second would ignore one of those earlier editions.

Givens: exactly one of the two statements is true. Statement 1: all levers in the box are steel. Statement 2: no lever in the box is steel.
If the box were empty, both statements would be true at once (a universal claim over zero levers holds vacuously), contradicting exactly one true.
So the box contains at least one lever.
With at least one lever: if all are steel, statement 1 is true and statement 2 false; if none is steel, statement 1 is false and statement 2 true. Both cases satisfy the condition, so which statement is the true one stays undetermined.
Result: the only conclusion forced in every allowed case is that the box holds at least one lever.
The tempting claim that the box is empty is exactly the case ruled out by the first deduction.

Givens: three tasks (triage, laboratory, records) assigned one each to Anil, Bea and Cara; Anil refuses triage; Cara refuses records.
Count by Cara's choice, since her refusal touches only records.
Case 1: Cara takes triage. Laboratory and records go to Anil and Bea in either order: 2 assignments.
Case 2: Cara takes laboratory. Triage and records remain; Anil refuses triage, so Anil takes records and Bea takes triage: 1 assignment.
Case 3 is impossible: Cara refuses records.
Result: 2 + 1 = 3 valid assignments.
The tempting 6 counts every permutation and ignores the two refusals; the tempting 2 stops after the first case.

Given: time 7:35; minute hand speed 6 degrees per minute; hour hand speed 30 degrees per hour plus 0.5 degrees per minute.
Relationship: measure each hand clockwise from 12, then subtract the two angles.
Substitute (minute hand): 35 × 6 = 210 degrees.
Substitute (hour hand): 7 × 30 + 35 × 0.5 = 210 + 17.5 = 227.5 degrees.
Difference: 227.5 − 210 = 17.5 degrees.
Result: 17.5 degrees between the hands.
Classic slip: 35 degrees comes from comparing 210 with 7 × 30 = 210 and forgetting that the hour hand has drifted 17.5 degrees past the 7.

Givens: mean pain scores 8, 5, 3, 3 at doses 0, 2.5, 5 and 10 mg.
From 0 to 2.5 mg the mean falls 8 → 5; from 2.5 to 5 mg it falls 5 → 3.
From 5 to 10 mg the mean stays at 3: the dose-response curve has flattened.
Result: the supported conclusion is that increasing the dose beyond 5 mg produces no further average reduction.
The trial recorded only pain scores, so the data contain no safety information and cannot identify an optimal dose.
The claim of no effect fails because the mean dropped from 8 to 3, and higher doses are not always better because the fall stops.

Given: a rise of 10 percent on day 1 and a fall of 10 percent on day 2; take a starting price of 100.
Relationship: successive percentage changes multiply as factors of the running price.
Substitute: 100 × 1.10 = 110 after the rise.
110 × 0.90 = 99 after the fall.
Result: 99 against a start of 100, a net decrease of 1 percent.
Cross-check: 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, which is 99 percent of the start, confirming the 1 percent loss.
Classic slip: adding 10 and −10 to reach no change forgets that the fall acts on the raised price 110, not on the original 100.

Given: class of 30; biology 18, chemistry 15, both 8.
Relationship: inclusion-exclusion, at least one subject = biology + chemistry − both, because the 8 shared students are counted twice in the raw sum.
Substitute: 18 + 15 = 33, then 33 − 8 = 25 students study at least one subject.
Neither = class total − union = 30 − 25 = 5.
Result: 5 students study neither subject.
Classic slip: 4 comes from computing 30 − 18 − 8, which treats the shared students as if they stood outside both subjects; the overlap belongs inside the union and is subtracted once when the union is formed.

Givens: father AB, so his gametes carry A or B; mother OO, so her gametes carry O only. Each child gets one allele from each parent.
Father's contribution: A with probability one half, B with probability one half. Mother's contribution: O always.
Combine: A + O gives AO (group A); B + O gives BO (group B), each with probability one half.
Result: every child is group A or group B, and groups AB and O are impossible in this pairing.
AB needs A and B together, but the mother can never supply either; O needs O from both parents, but the father never supplies O.
The tempting claim that the children's groups cannot be predicted fails: the outcome set is fully determined, only the A-or-B split is fifty-fifty.

Givens: genes A and B on the same chromosome, no crossing over between them; cross AB/ab × ab/ab.
No crossing over means each homologue is passed on intact: the AB/ab parent makes exactly two gamete types, AB and ab, each with probability one half.
The tester ab/ab makes only ab gametes.
Combine: AB + ab gives AB/ab; ab + ab gives ab/ab, in a 1:1 ratio.
Result: only the two parental types appear, in equal proportions.
The classic 1:1:1:1 testcross ratio needs the recombinant gametes Ab and aB, which cannot be produced without crossing over.

Given: mother XᴴXʰ (carrier), father XʰY (affected).
Relationship: every daughter receives the father's only X chromosome (Xʰ); she additionally receives Xᴴ or Xʰ from the mother with probability one half each.
Substitute: daughter genotypes are XᴴXʰ (carrier) with probability 1/2 and XʰXʰ (affected) with probability 1/2.
Result: 1/2 of the daughters are expected to have haemophilia.
Classic slip: 1/4 is the fraction among all children, because it folds in the separate 1/2 chance of being a daughter at all; the question asks only about daughters.

The decisive fact: a guanine-cytosine pair is joined by three hydrogen bonds, while an adenine-thymine pair has only two. This is why GC-rich DNA needs more heat to separate. The bonds are hydrogen bonds, not covalent links between the strands.

Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that copies the viral RNA genome into DNA, which then integrates into the host chromosome. The host's own DNA polymerase copies DNA templates, not RNA, and RNA polymerase makes RNA from DNA, the wrong direction for this step.

Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel. Reading the codon 5'-AUG-3', the pairing runs A with U, U with A, G with C, so the anticodon written in the 3' to 5' direction is 3'-UAC-5'. Written in the 5' to 3' direction the same anticodon would read CAU, and any sequence containing T cannot be right because tRNA is RNA.

Quaternary structure means an assembly of more than one polypeptide chain. Haemoglobin, with its four subunits (two alpha and two beta chains), is the textbook example. Myoglobin, pepsin and ribonuclease are each a single chain and so show at most tertiary structure, while an alpha-helix is a motif of secondary structure, not a whole protein organisation.

The amino group of one amino acid attacks the carboxyl group of the other; one molecule of water is released and a peptide (amide) bond forms. This is a condensation reaction. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, breaking the bond by adding water, so the option describing hydrolysis with water consumed gets the direction of the reaction backwards.

Fermentation is glycolysis plus the regeneration of NAD+, and it stops at reduced end-products such as lactate or ethanol. The glucose carbon is never fully oxidised to CO2 and water, and the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain never run, so almost all of the glucose's energy remains locked in the end-products. The 2 ATP that are made all come from glycolysis, so fermentation certainly does produce ATP.

Substrate-level phosphorylation is direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP. It occurs at two steps of glycolysis (the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps) and at one step of the Krebs cycle (succinyl-CoA synthetase). The electron transport chain instead uses oxidative phosphorylation through a proton gradient, which is why the option naming it is wrong.

Chlorophyll's absorption peaks strongly in the blue and red regions of the spectrum; green light is largely reflected and transmitted, so that is the light reaching our eyes and leaves look green. The claim that it absorbs only green light inverts the truth (leaves would then appear the complementary colour), and absorbing all wavelengths equally would make leaves look black.

The sodium-potassium pump (Na+/K+-ATPase) hydrolyses one ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+, each ion moved against its gradient. This electrogenic imbalance (net loss of one positive charge per cycle) contributes to the resting potential and keeps the ionic gradients that nerve and muscle firing consume. The ratio 3 out : 2 in at a cost of one ATP is the only version matching the textbook pump.

The G2 checkpoint sits after S phase and before mitosis, and it verifies that DNA replication is complete and that any damage is repaired before the cell commits to division. The G1 checkpoint decides whether to begin a new cycle (cell size, nutrients, DNA integrity at the start), and the spindle checkpoint acts inside mitosis at metaphase, too late to check replication.

In both meiosis II and mitosis, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles, so the mechanics of segregation are the same. Pairing of homologues, crossing over, halving of the chromosome number and alignment of bivalents on the equator are all features of meiosis I, and the cell first becomes haploid at the end of meiosis I, already before meiosis II begins.

At rest the membrane is most permeable to potassium through open K+ leak channels. Potassium diffuses out down its concentration gradient, leaving behind unbalanced intracellular negative charge (large fixed anions that cannot follow), and this builds the resting potential of about minus 70 mV. The pump maintains the gradients over time, but its 3-out : 2-in imbalance is only a minor direct contributor to the voltage.

A reflex arc runs: receptor detects the stimulus, sensory (afferent) neurone carries the signal to the CNS, integration occurs in the centre, motor (efferent) neurone carries the command outward, and the effector (muscle or gland) responds. Every sequence that puts the motor neurone before the CNS, or the CNS before the receptor, reverses the direction of information flow.

The decisive fact: adrenaline, released from the adrenal medulla as part of the acute fight-or-flight response, stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver and raises blood glucose to fuel rapid action. Insulin lowers blood glucose (the opposite direction), ADH and aldosterone regulate water and sodium balance rather than glucose, and oxytocin concerns labour and milk ejection.

A live attenuated vaccine delivers an artificially introduced but weakened microbe that multiplies slightly and provokes a genuine primary immune response, generating the person's own plasma cells and memory cells: active, artificially acquired immunity. Passive immunity would mean receiving ready-made antibodies, which is not what a vaccine injects, and the fact that the pathogen is weakened does not stop it from being immunogenic, which is the whole point of attenuation.

The sinoatrial node, a small region in the wall of the right atrium, depolarises fastest of all cardiac cells and initiates each heartbeat, making it the natural pacemaker. The atrioventricular node is only the normal relay to the ventricles, and the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres conduct the impulse onward; the vagus nerve modulates the rate but does not set the rhythm.

Diffusion efficiency scales with surface area divided by wall thickness. Hundreds of millions of alveoli provide roughly 70 square metres of exchange surface behind walls of extremely thin squamous cells (about half a micrometre), which is the structural basis of their efficiency. Alveoli have no muscle to pump air, no cartilage rings (those are in the larger airways), and they store no oxygen.

ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct cells and triggers insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into their membrane, so water leaves the filtrate down the medullary osmotic gradient and urine becomes concentrated. It does not act by changing filtration pressure, opening sodium channels, or constricting the efferent arteriole; it is a water-permeability hormone.

Each PCR cycle starts with a denaturation step near 95 degrees Celsius that separates the DNA strands, and this step repeats dozens of times. An ordinary polymerase would be inactivated after the first few cycles, so a heat-stable polymerase such as Taq (from hot-spring bacteria) is needed to survive the whole programme. It is the high-temperature strand-separation step, not low temperature, that demands the special enzyme.

This is selective toxicity: because bacterial ribosomes are 70S while the patient's own cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, the drug can shut down bacterial protein synthesis without directly stopping protein synthesis in the patient's cells. It is not side-effect free at any dose, since human mitochondria carry their own 70S-like ribosomes and can be secondarily affected, and the drug targets bacteria, not viruses or mitochondria alone.

Given: methanol CH₃OH, a neutral molecule; standard values H = +1, O = −2.
Relationship: in a neutral molecule the oxidation numbers sum to 0.
Substitute: C + 4 × (+1) + (−2) = 0.
Arithmetic: C + 4 − 2 = 0, so C + 2 = 0.
Result: carbon is at −2.
Classic slip: +4 is the oxidation number of the carbon in CO₂, reached by counting oxygens instead of hydrogens; +2 belongs to an aldehyde carbon, one oxidation step above methanol.

Given: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O; chlorine starts as the element, oxidation number 0; Na is +1 and O is −2 throughout the products.
In NaCl the chlorine sits at −1 (plain chloride).
In NaOCl: +1 + Cl + (−2) = 0, so Cl = +1.
One chlorine atom has gone 0 → −1 (gained an electron, reduced); the other has gone 0 → +1 (lost an electron, oxidised).
Result: the same element is oxidised and reduced in the same reaction, a disproportionation.
The tempting reduced-only or oxidised-only readings each cover just one of the two products; unchanged fails because the oxidation numbers demonstrably leave 0.

BF3 is trigonal planar: three identical polar B-F bonds point symmetrically at 120 degrees, so their dipoles cancel vectorially and the molecule has zero net dipole despite the polar bonds. In NH3 (trigonal pyramidal), H2O and SO2 (both bent) and CHCl3 (an asymmetric tetrahedron) the bond dipoles do not cancel, leaving a permanent net dipole.

NH3 has three bonding pairs plus one lone pair on nitrogen. The tetrahedral electron arrangement leaves the molecular shape trigonal pyramidal with a bond angle of about 107 degrees. CH4 (no lone pairs) is tetrahedral, H2O (two lone pairs) is bent, BF3 is trigonal planar and CO2 is linear.

Given: c = 0.005 M Ba(OH)₂; each formula unit releases 2 OH⁻; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.
Relationship: [OH⁻] = 2 × c; pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; pH = 14 − pOH.
Substitute: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.005 = 0.010 mol/L.
pOH = −log(0.010) = 2.
pH = 14 − 2 = 12.
Result: pH 12.
Classic slip: ignoring the factor 2 gives [OH⁻] = 0.005 M, pOH ≈ 2.3 and pH ≈ 11.7, the tempting value near 11; and the intermediate 2 is the pOH, not the pH.

Given: solution A at pH 4, solution B at pH 6.
Relationship: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so each 1-unit step in pH is a factor of 10 in hydrogen ion concentration.
Substitute: [H⁺] of A = 10⁻⁴ mol/L; [H⁺] of B = 10⁻⁶ mol/L.
Ratio: 10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10² = 100.
Result: A's hydrogen ion concentration is 100 times greater than B's.
Classic slip: 2 times greater reads the 2-unit pH gap as a linear factor, but the scale is logarithmic.

Given: n = 0.25 mol of CO₂; Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; each CO₂ molecule contains 3 atoms (1 carbon + 2 oxygen).
Relationship: molecules = n × Nₐ, then total atoms = molecules × 3.
Substitute: 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.5 × 10²³ molecules.
Multiply by 3: 3 × 1.5 × 10²³ = 4.5 × 10²³ atoms.
Result: 4.5 × 10²³ atoms in total.
Classic slip: stopping at 1.5 × 10²³ reports molecules, not atoms; counting only one oxygen (×2 per molecule) gives 3.0 × 10²³.

Given: 10.0 g of pure CaCO₃ (M = 100 g/mol) releases 2.24 L of CO₂ at STP; the impure 10.0 g sample releases 1.68 L at STP.
Relationship: CO₂ volume is directly proportional to the amount of CaCO₃ present, so the purity fraction equals the volume ratio.
Substitute: purity = 1.68 ÷ 2.24 = 0.75.
Convert: 0.75 × 100 = 75 percent.
Result: the sample is 75 percent CaCO₃.
Classic slip: 25 percent divides the missing volume 0.56 ÷ 2.24 and so measures the impurity, not the carbonate; 133 percent inverts the ratio and is impossible for a percentage.

Given: P₁ = 1.0 atm; T₁ = 27 °C; T₂ = 127 °C; rigid vessel, so volume and amount are constant.
Relationship: Gay-Lussac's law, P₂ = P₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁, valid only in absolute temperature.
Convert: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K.
Substitute: P₂ = 1.0 × 400 ÷ 300.
Arithmetic: 400 ÷ 300 = 1.33.
Result: the new pressure is about 1.33 atm.
Classic slip: inverting the ratio (300 ÷ 400) predicts a pressure fall from heating, which is unphysical; dividing 127 by 27 in plain Celsius is meaningless because the Celsius zero is arbitrary.

Sodium and chlorine belong to the same period, so both have their outer electrons in the same third shell. Chlorine's nucleus carries 17 protons against sodium's 11, and this greater nuclear charge pulls the same-shell electrons closer, making the atom smaller. The comparison concerns neutral atoms, so ion formation is irrelevant, and the shell count is identical, not higher, for chlorine.

An alcohol and a carboxylic acid under reflux with concentrated sulfuric acid undergo esterification. The alcohol supplies the alkyl part (methanol gives methyl) and the acid supplies the carboxylate part (propanoic acid gives propanoate), so the product is methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3, with water as by-product. The reverse name (propanyl-type esters) or any aldehyde or anhydride misreads which fragment comes from which reagent.

Hydrogen bromide adds to propene by Markovnikov's rule: H attaches to the double-bond carbon that already has more hydrogens (the terminal CH2), because that route passes through the more stable secondary carbocation, and Br then bonds to the middle carbon. The product is 2-bromopropane, CH3-CHBr-CH3. The bromine on the end carbon (1-bromopropane) would be the anti-Markovnikov product, obtained only in the presence of peroxides, and the dibromide would need Br2 rather than HBr.

In a heterogeneous equilibrium the pure solids appear in fixed amounts, so their terms are constants that are folded into the equilibrium constant and omitted from the expression. Only the gaseous product remains: Kc = [CO2]. Including the solids in a quotient, or inverting the expression, misapplies the rule that pure phases are excluded.

In any working galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode, and the electrons released travel through the external wire from anode to cathode, where reduction takes place. The salt bridge carries ions, never electrons, and its anions migrate toward the anode compartment to neutralise the positive charge building up there (cations drift toward the cathode side). Any statement that puts oxidation at the cathode, or electrons in the bridge, contradicts these roles.

Given: four solutions, each 0.10 M: glucose C₆H₁₂O₆, NaCl, CaCl₂, sucrose.
Relationship: freezing-point depression is colligative, set by the number of dissolved particles per litre, not their identity.
Count particles: glucose and sucrose do not ionise, 0.10 mol of particles per litre each.
NaCl gives 2 ions per formula unit: 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 mol of particles per litre.
CaCl₂ gives 3 ions per formula unit: 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 mol of particles per litre.
Result: the greatest particle count gives the greatest depression, so the CaCl₂ solution freezes lowest.
Classic slip: all four freezing together assumes equal molarity means equal effect, but only particle counts decide; NaCl's 0.20 loses to CaCl₂'s 0.30.

Given: 8 − 5x < −12.
Isolate the x term: subtract 8 from both sides, −5x < −12 − 8, so −5x < −20.
Divide both sides by −5: division by a negative number flips the direction, so x > 4.
Check: at x = 5, 8 − 5 × 5 = 8 − 25 = −17, and −17 < −12 holds.
Result: x > 4.
Classic slip: dividing by −5 without flipping gives x < 4, the exact reverse set; x = 4 itself fails because 8 − 20 = −12 is not strictly less than −12, so the loose bound of 4 or more is wrong too.

Given: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7.
Subtract 1 from all three parts: −4 < 2x ≤ 6.
Divide all three parts by 2, a positive number, so both directions and strictness survive: −2 < x ≤ 3.
Result: −2 < x ≤ 3.
Classic slip: making the left bound inclusive (−2 ≤ x) forgets that the original −3 was strict; testing x = −2 gives −3 on the left, which fails.

Given: 2ˣ = 40.
Relationship: 2ˣ rises continuously with x, so bracket 40 between neighbouring whole-number powers.
Compute: 2⁵ = 32 and 2⁶ = 64.
Compare: 32 < 40 < 64, so x sits strictly between 5 and 6.
Result: 5 < x < 6 (exactly log₂ 40 ≈ 5.32).
Classic slip: x = 5 or x = 6 would require 40 to equal 32 or 64, which it does not.

Given: one card drawn from a standard 52-card deck; wanted: heart or king.
Relationship: inclusion-exclusion, favourable = hearts + kings − cards counted in both sets.
Count: 13 hearts; 4 kings; the king of hearts lies in both, so subtract 1.
Favourable = 13 + 4 − 1 = 16.
Probability = 16 ÷ 52 = 4/13.
Result: 4/13.
Classic slip: 17/52 adds 13 + 4 and never removes the king of hearts, which is simultaneously a heart and a king.

Given: ramp length (hypotenuse) 8 m; angle with the horizontal 30°; sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87.
Relationship: in a right triangle the side opposite an angle equals hypotenuse × sin(angle); the height is opposite the 30° angle.
Substitute: height = 8 × sin 30° = 8 × 0.5.
Arithmetic: 8 × 0.5 = 4.
Result: the upper end of the ramp is 4 m above the ground.
Classic slip: 6.9 m comes from 8 × cos 30° = 8 × 0.87, which is the ramp's horizontal reach along the ground, not the vertical rise.

Given: f(x) = 2x − 1; wanted f(f(x)).
Relationship: composition feeds the inner output back into f as the input.
Substitute: f(f(x)) = 2 × (2x − 1) − 1.
Expand: 4x − 2 − 1.
Collect: 4x − 3.
Result: f(f(x)) = 4x − 3.
Classic slip: 2x − 3 doubles only once; both the doubling and the subtraction happen at each of the two passes through f.

Given: (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 16.
Relationship: standard circle form (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², centre (h, k), radius r.
Match: x − 1 = x − h gives h = 1; y + 2 = y − (−2) gives k = −2.
Radius: r² = 16, so r = √16 = 4.
Result: centre (1, −2), radius 4.
Classic slip: reading the plus sign in y + 2 as k = +2 puts the centre in the wrong quadrant, and quoting 16 as the radius confuses r² with r.

Given: V = 24 V battery; 2 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 12 Ω and 6 Ω.
Relationship: parallel pair via 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; series resistances add; Ohm's law I = V ÷ R.
Substitute: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/6; with 1/6 = 2/12 this gives 1/R = 3/12.
Invert: R = 12/3 = 4 Ω.
Add the series resistor: 2 + 4 = 6 Ω total.
Substitute into Ohm's law: I = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 A.
Result: 4 A flows from the battery.
Classic slip: 2 A comes from 24 ÷ 12, which ignores the parallel section; 6 A comes from 24 ÷ 4, which forgets the series 2 Ω.

Given: P = 60 W, V = 120 V.
Relationship: P = V² ÷ R, rearranged as R = V² ÷ P.
Substitute: R = 120² ÷ 60.
Square: 120² = 14400.
Divide: 14400 ÷ 60 = 240.
Result: the filament resistance is 240 Ω.
Classic slip: 2 Ω comes from V ÷ P = 120 ÷ 60, which actually computes the current the lamp draws, not the resistance.

Givens: water boiling at atmospheric pressure; flame supplies heat continuously; thermometer stays at exactly 100 °C.
Once boiling starts, added energy no longer increases the molecules' average kinetic energy, so the temperature cannot rise.
Every joule goes into the latent heat of vaporisation (about 2260 J per gram), pulling molecules apart against their intermolecular attractions.
A phase change in progress is isothermal: the reading stays pinned until the last liquid has evaporated.
Result: the temperature holds at 100 °C because the heat is consumed by the phase change itself.
The tempting claim that the molecules stop moving fails: they are in fact receiving the energy needed to break free as vapour.

Givens: a crash fixes the change of momentum Δp the car must undergo; impulse relation F × Δt = Δp.
The crumple zone deforms on impact, stretching the collision time Δt.
Rearrange: F = Δp ÷ Δt; with Δp fixed and Δt longer, the average force F shrinks.
Result: the same momentum change is delivered by a smaller average force on the occupants, and injury scales with force.
The tempting claims fail because the impulse is neither eliminated nor increased: Δp is set by the crash, only the time over which it is delivered changes.

Givens: a distance-time graph with a horizontal segment.
On a distance-time graph the gradient of the line is the speed, since speed = distance covered ÷ time taken.
A horizontal segment has zero gradient: zero rise in distance during the interval.
Zero distance covered means zero speed, so the object is stationary for that interval.
Result: a horizontal segment on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary.
The tempting reading of constant non-zero speed comes from importing the rule for velocity-time graphs, where a flat line does mean steady speed; read the axis label first.

Given: block density ρ_block = 0.90 g/cm³; water density ρ_water = 1.00 g/cm³; block volume V, submerged volume V_sub.
Relationship: floating equilibrium, weight = upthrust: ρ_block × V × g = ρ_water × V_sub × g.
Cancel g from both sides, then cancel V: V_sub ÷ V = ρ_block ÷ ρ_water = 0.90 ÷ 1.00.
Arithmetic: 0.90 ÷ 1.00 = 0.90.
Result: 0.90, so 90 percent of the block's volume is submerged.
Classic slip: 10 percent is the fraction above water, the complement of the submerged share; the submerged fraction tracks the density ratio itself.
